UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms : 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
POST-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE COMMENTS OF THE 
PJM INDUSTRIAL CUSTOMER COALITION 
The PJM Industrial Customer Coalition (“PJMICC” or “the Coalition”) respectfully 
submits these post-technical conference comments in response to the Supplemental Notice issued 
by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”) on July 30, 2026, in 
the above-captioned proceeding. PJMICC is a coalition of energy-intensive industrial and 
institutional customers and is active in the governance and stakeholder process of PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. ("PJM"). PJMICC members have invested billions of dollars in their 
manufacturing and other energy-intensive operations and are directly affected by the cost and 
reliability consequences of PJM’s decisions. 
PJMICC submits these Post-Technical Conference comments following the July 23, 2026, 
technical conference and in anticipation of the upcoming Alternative Dispute Resolution (“ADR”) 
process at the Commission and potential future Commission action with respect to PJM.1 PJMICC 
is considering PJM’s initial mediation term sheet and the proposed Memorandum of 
Understanding (“MOU”) Framework with the states, which were publicly posted in anticipation 
of the PJM Members Committee meeting on August 19, 2026.2 PJMICC approaches the upcoming 
 
1 PJMICC's counsel, Susan Bruce, participated in the Technical Conference and filed a Pre-filed Statement.  PJMICC 
will not reiterate those positions in these Post-Technical Conference Comments, but offers these comments as a 
constructive response to the Technical Conference and PJM’s recent proposed term sheets offered in advance of the 
upcoming ADR.  
2 See 20260819-item-08---1-ferc-mediation-term-sheet.pdf and https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-

pjm-and-states.pdf (last visited Aug. 21, 2026).

2 
mediation in good faith and recognizes the constructive engagement of PJM, the PJM states, and 
PJM Members to date. 
To that end, PJMICC highlights the PJM Members Committee's August 19 action to 
approve, by a substantial margin, modifications to the PJM Operating Agreement clarifying that 
the PJM Board’s primary responsibilities include “designing and operating markets that benefit 
customers.”3 This modification, if filed and accepted by the Commission, aligns closely with 
PJMICC’s recommended change to the PJM Operating Agreement outlined in its Pre-filed 
Statement and represents a constructive step toward grounding the Board’s future decision-making 
in that responsibility.4  
Given the important role PJM plays in the region’s economy and daily life, PJMICC’s 
objective is to advance governance reforms that enhance PJM’s accountability and independence, 
improve the efficiency of the stakeholder process, reduce siloed consideration of related issues, 
advance innovation, and ensure that diverse viewpoints inform the region’s response to this period 
of foundational change. In these comments, PJMICC identifies areas of alignment with PJM's 
initial position set forth at the July 23 technical conference, as well as areas of focus to build 
understanding in advance of the ADR process. 
PJMICC respectfully submits that any governance reform package should preserve the 
existing balance between PJM’s independent role and the Members Committee’s sector-weighted 
approval of Section 205 filings. PJM retains a path to seek Commission action when Members do

vistra--exelon-alternate-motion-to-arrc-user-group-oa-sec-7.pdf; https://www.pjm.com/-

1b.pdf (last visited Aug. 21, 2026). 
4 Pre-Filed Statement of Susan Bruce, Counsel to PJM Industrial Customer Coalition, PJM Governance and 
Stakeholder Reforms, Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 4 (July 14, 2026).

3 
not agree; as discussed below, Section 206 provides the appropriate framework in that 
circumstance. The Coalition’s focus is therefore on reforms that improve stakeholder efficiency 
and pair any expansion of PJM’s authority with transparent safeguards, while respecting Board 
independence. 
I. 
Background 
On July 23, 2026, the Commission convened a Chairman and Commissioner-led technical 
conference to examine PJM’s governance structure and stakeholder processes, addressing Board 
independence, Section 205 filing rights, stakeholder process reform, and state participation. The 
Commission invited post-conference comments on or before August 21, 2026, and indicated that 
an Alternative Dispute Resolution process will commence on September 1, 2026. 
Through its counsel, PJMICC participated in the July 23 technical conference, emphasizing 
support for PJM’s existing governance framework and sector-weighted voting; advocating 
targeted reform rather than wholesale restructuring, including reforms that would facilitate new 
resources and investment in the PJM grid; and identifying the need for customer cost-impact 
assessments and after-the-fact review mechanisms. 
Subsequently, PJM circulated its mediation term sheet proposing eight reform measures, 
including proposing to assume from PJM Members additional Section 205 filing authority, making 
the Members Committee advisory to the RTO on all matters, extending Board terms to nine years, 
and creating state “jump ball” Section 205 filing rights regarding resource adequacy. PJM also 
proposed an MOU Framework with the states that addresses resource adequacy, large-load 
management, and transmission planning.

4 
II. 
Areas of Common Ground 
PJMICC supports PJM’s willingness to streamline committee structures and create 
expedited processes, provided that the process continues to solicit and consider diverse viewpoints. 
These proposals are directionally consistent with PJMICC’s longstanding concerns about siloed 
treatment of related issues and the cost of engagement in the stakeholder process for those with 
limited resources. The proposed elimination of the Markets and Reliability Committee, coupled 
with the proposed shift in voting at lower-level committees to sector-weighted voting, represents 
a reasonable balance. Taken together, eliminating duplicative committee-layer changes could 
improve efficiency while preserving meaningful stakeholder input and the sector-weighted 
framework. This would allow stakeholders to focus on consequential issues. 
PJMICC also supports Board independence as a foundational element of PJM governance. 
PJM’s proposal for open Board sessions—with public statements and recorded votes—generally 
aligns with PJMICC’s transparency goals, while warranting careful implementation to preserve 
the Board’s independence. Extended Board terms, if paired with meaningful accountability 
measures, could promote institutional stability, although a nine-year term may be longer than 
necessary and could discourage interest in Board service.  Board members for the other RTOs and 
ISOs across the country have three-year terms.  Board terms of five or six years are still longer 
than those of other RTOs/ISOs. 
III.  
Areas of Divergence 
While acknowledging this common ground, PJMICC also identifies areas of divergence 
that warrant attention in developing a durable solution. Of particular importance is the relationship 
between PJM’s proposed Section 205 filing rights and the stakeholder checks that currently govern 
those rights.

5 
PJM’s mediation term sheet proposes removing PJM Members’ Section 205 filing 
authority over the energy and ancillary services markets, as well as transmission planning. The 
term sheet also proposes making the Members Committee advisory on RTO functions, extending 
Board terms to nine years, and providing that PJM-sponsored packages advance “on equal footing” 
with stakeholder alternatives. PJM currently holds Section 205 rights regarding resource adequacy 
and the capacity construct.  The areas of concern with the PJM capacity construct are well 
documented in proceedings before this Commission.   
PJM’s proposals, taken together, raise significant concerns. As explained in PJMICC’s Pre-
filed Statement at this docket, the distinction between Section 205 and Section 206 review is not 
merely procedural—it reflects a deliberate allocation of regulatory burdens that incentivizes 
collaborative development of market rules.5 The question presented is not whether PJM can act 
when Members do not agree—it can, through Section 206—but rather which review standard 
should apply, and what safeguards should attend the expansion of unilateral filing authority. 
As outlined in PJMICC’s Pre-filed Statement, the D.C. Circuit has recognized that Sections 
205 and 206, while both requiring just and reasonable rates, “enforce that mandate differently” 
and impose distinct burdens on proponents of rate changes.6 The lighter Section 205 burden is 
appropriately reserved for proposals that command broad stakeholder support and provide 
evidence of balanced consideration of competing interests. Where that support is absent, Section 
206 supplies the appropriate review framework—not as a bar on PJM action, but as a check 
commensurate with the significance of unilateral change that could directly affect the regional 
economy. 
 
5 Pre-Filed Statement of Susan Bruce, Counsel to PJM Industrial Customer Coalition, PJM Governance and 
Stakeholder Reforms, Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 7-8 (July 14, 2026).  
6 Md. Office of People's Couns. v. FERC, 164 F.4th 920, 923 (D.C. Cir. 2026).

6 
PJM’s proposal to make the Members Committee advisory on RTO functions would 
represent a significant shift from the current framework.  PJMICC views the Members 
Committee's approval as an important check on PJM management and Board actions. If 
stakeholders were limited to a consultative role while PJM’s unilateral authority expanded, the 
reform package would reduce a meaningful source of accountability. For example, there can be an 
inherent tension in RTO governance when staff or management advance positions that may diverge 
from the broader public interest the Board is charged with serving. That tension is compounded by 
the specialized operational and technical expertise of RTO staff, which independent Board 
members—despite their experience and best efforts—may not fully share. PJMICC respectfully 
suggests that maintaining a meaningful role for the Members Committee would preserve a 
diversity of sector perspectives at a point when the Board may benefit most from them.  These 
areas of divergence underscore the need to examine the accountability framework that would 
accompany any expansion of PJM’s authority. 
IV.  
Accountability Considerations  
A central concern animating these comments is what may be viewed as an “accountability 
gap” in PJM’s reform proposals. PJM has explained that expanded Section 205 filing rights would 
help it act decisively when the stakeholder process does not produce timely outcomes.  At the same 
time, the term sheet does not include comparable mechanisms for evaluating the consequences of 
PJM’s decisions, such as customer cost-impact assessments, structured after-the-fact reviews, or 
sunset provisions. Unlike a conventional utility, PJM generally does not internalize the financial 
consequences of its market-design decisions; PJM Members, states, and customers bear the effects.  
While PJMICC does not support PJM securing additional Section 205 rights, PJMICC does see 
value in implementing additional accountability safeguards that make performance and customer

7 
impacts visible and provide a basis for corrective action. The governance literature identifies this 
risk allocation as presenting a structural asymmetry.7  
These observations underscore additional authority, to the extent directed by the 
Commission or otherwise, should be accompanied by transparent projections, defined success 
metrics, and a structured opportunity to adjust course when results differ from expectations.  PJM’s 
own proposed reforms—longer Board terms, an advisory role for the Members Committee, and 
expanded filing authority—would increase the Board’s independence while reducing certain 
traditional stakeholder checks. That combination warrants careful design: the governance literature 
identifies structural incentive considerations that may affect independent Boards.8  
The need for a constructive accountability framework is particularly important given the 
PJM region’s unprecedented challenges—large load growth, manufacturing reshoring, data center 
development, and electrification mandates. Decisions made now will shape the cost landscape for 
decades. PJMICC therefore supports objective, transparent accountability measures that 
complement—not compromise—Board independence, including Board evaluations tied to 
customer outcomes, affordability, and the cost consequences of PJM’s decisions.   
V.  
Proposed Accountability Safeguards 
To address the considerations identified above, PJMICC respectfully proposes the 
following measures to complement any governance reform package.  They are designed to operate 
consistently with Board independence while providing transparent, objective methods for 
evaluating the effects of any expanded authority on retail customers and the public interest. 
 
7 See Dworkin & Goldwasser, Governance of RTOs, 28 ENERGY L.J. 543, 580–81 (2007). 
8 See id. at 562; James et al., How the RTO Stakeholder Process Affects Market Efficiency, R STREET POLICY STUDY 
No. 112, at 11, 17–18 (2017).

8 
Board Composition. The Coalition recommends that PJM’s Board include members with 
direct experience managing large energy budgets or overseeing industrial and commercial energy 
consumers, ensuring that demand-side perspectives inform Board deliberations. This perspective 
would supplement, not displace, Board independence by bringing relevant customer experience 
into informed deliberations. 
Mandatory Ex Post Reviews. Any significant market or transmission rule change should 
be subject to mandatory after-the-fact review to assess whether it delivered its intended results, 
including actual cost impacts on customers. Where a rule change fails to deliver its intended 
benefits or produces cost impacts that materially exceed projections, the reform package should 
include defined corrective measures, which may include a sunset or reversion. 
Corporate Transparency. PJM should disclose greater information regarding corporate 
goals and executive compensation structures, including public performance metrics tied to 
customer outcomes and cost management. Transparency into institutional incentives would enable 
stakeholders and the Commission to evaluate whether those incentives appropriately balance 
reliability, customer cost, competition, and responsible cost management.  This level of 
transparency is especially necessary to the extent that PJM were to be afforded Section 205 rights. 
Customer Cost-Impact Assessments. Customer cost-impact statements, including robust 
stress testing, should be required for any significant Section 205 (and Section 206) filing by PJM. 
Analogous to regulatory impact analyses, these assessments would identify expected effects on 
end-use customers and the assumptions underlying the proposal. Making that information 
available would help the Commission and affected customers evaluate the proposal’s likely 
consequences and support informed review.

9 
Together, these safeguards—Demand-Side Board expertise, ex post reviews, corporate 
transparency, and cost-impact assessments—would help to ensure PJM’s expanded authority is 
exercised accountably and in the public interest.

10 
VI.  
Conclusion 
PJMICC supports meaningful governance reform and appreciates the Commission’s 
leadership and the constructive engagement of PJM, the PJM states, and PJM Members. 
Particularly at this inflection point, the need for clear-eyed focus on the reforms necessary to 
support cost-effective investment in the PJM grid, PJMICC’s principal recommendation is to 
preserve the existing distinction between Section 205 and Section 206 and the associated 
regulatory rigor, with additional transparent, objective accountability safeguards. 
PJMICC respectfully urges the Commission to consider the safeguards described above—
including transparent cost assessments, defined success metrics, ex post review with appropriate 
corrective measures, demand-side Board expertise, and corporate transparency—into any final 
governance package. These measures would support durable reform, protect meaningful 
stakeholder participation, and help ensure that PJM’s governance serves the public interest while 
respecting Board independence. 
Respectfully submitted, 
By: 
/s/ Susan E. Bruce

APPENDIX 
 
PJM Industrial Customer Coalition (“PJMICC”) has actively participated in the PJM 
stakeholder process since its inception as an independent system operator (“ISO”).  Eight 
of PJMICC’s approximately 30 members are part of the End-Use Customer sector to 
participate in the PJM governance process.  A subset of these PJMICC PJM Members have 
also become PJM Members to support their own business activities, such as demand 
response, load-serving approaches, and, as retail customers with behind-the-meter 
generation, to sell excess power produced by their cogeneration facilities.  PJMICC’s 
membership also includes a PJM Member in the Generation Owner sector because its on-
site generation in the PJM footprint exceeds its load.

Should Board members’ terms be extended to five or more years? 
X 
 
 
Comments: Board member terms of five to six years would be appropriate for 
building deeper institutional knowledge, strengthening relationships, and 
supporting continuity.  Terms of much longer than that risk entrenchment and 
reduce opportunities for accountability. 
2) 
Should there be a maximum number of years that a Board 
member may serve (e.g., 10 years)? 
X 
 
 
Comments: In good board governance, term limits are a best practice to prevent 
stagnation and bring in new ideas.  Given the complexity of RTOs, it may be 
appropriate to have longer terms than conventional corporate boards, but the 
principle still holds. 
3) 
Should the Board member qualification rules be revised to provide 
a preference for some Board members that reside in the PJM 
region? 
X 
 
 
Comments:  Yes, provided that conflict of interest considerations are also 
honored. 
4) 
Should the conflict-of-interest rules be revised to reduce the 
cooling-off period for Board members from two years to one 
year? 
X 
 
 
Comments: For RTO independence, the conflict of interest rules are vital, but 
there is no meaningful difference between one and two years of a cooling-off 
period for appropriate Board candidates.

5) 
Should restrictions on Board communications be relaxed to enable 
more communication between the Board and stakeholders? 
 
X 
 
Comments:  There are currently ample opportunities for communication between 
the PJM Board and stakeholders; relaxing the restrictions risks the perceptions of 
“back door dealings” among powerful interests. 
6) 
In order to increase transparency, should Board votes be made 
public or the Board be required to explain its reasoning? 
X 
 
 
Comments:  To advance Board independence, PJMICC is concerned about 
individual Board votes being made public; however, PJMICC supports the Board 
being required to explain its reasoning and engage meaningfully with minority 
positions that were adopted. 
7) 
In order to increase transparency, should some Board meetings be 
open or available to the public? 
X 
 
 
Comments:  A qualified answer:  While PJMICC does not support all Board 
meetings being public, some additional transparency on the information on which 
the Board bases its decision would be beneficial.  For example, it would be 
helpful to know how the Board assesses PJM staff proposals vis-à-vis stakeholder 
proposals. 
8) 
Should PJM’s governing documents be revised to explicitly state 
that the responsibility of PJM and its Board is to serve the public 
interest? 
X 
 
 
Comments:  PJMICC also supports revising the PJM’s governing documents to 
explicitly state that PJM’s markets and planning should be designed and operated 
to cost-effectively support the functioning of retail jurisdictions' provision of 
electric service to consumers. 
9)

the Nominating Committee?
